title: Making connections through retrieval: An example
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino, a science teacher, argues that retrieval practice only supports transfer when it is designed to connect new learning to prior knowledge rather than serving as a box-ticking starter. She admits her own earlier habit of asking five basic recall questions that offered no chance of application, and wonders why students still struggled with respiration. Using an introduction to respiration as a worked example, she lists the fourteen pieces of prerequisite knowledge students need secure, from the energy stored in food to the function of mitochondria, and then walks through how she would sequence the lesson so that each step retrieves and reuses earlier concepts. Along the way she makes concrete pedagogical decisions: precise vocabulary such as glucose rather than food, skipping etymology when it would blur the difference between respiration and breathing, modelling equation balancing explicitly when students have not met it, and pre-empting cognitive overload by retrieving energy stores a few lessons earlier. The piece is a detailed, practitioner-level illustration of retrieval, spacing and cognitive load working together toward transfer.
points: Castelino's core claim is that retrieval must involve application and connection, since five recall questions at the start of a lesson can feel rigorous while building no transfer.
Her respiration example begins by listing the prerequisite knowledge students must have secure, which turns lesson planning into mapping what must be retrieved before the new idea arrives.
She treats prior concepts such as energy stores and combustion as bridges, transferring them from physics and chemistry to a biology topic rather than teaching respiration in isolation.
Cognitive load shapes her sequencing: if prior knowledge is stale, she retrieves it a few lessons earlier so working memory is not overloaded during the new lesson.
Small precision choices, using glucose instead of food and skipping an unhelpful etymology, are presented as deliberate moves to prevent confusion between respiration and breathing.
quotes: Retrieval does not simply entail asking 5 questions at the start or end of a lesson. I am guilty of doing just this. Even worse, the questions were very basic recall questions with no chance of application.

Usually, I am a big fan of discussing etymology when I introduce a new word. In this case, I wouldn’t bother as respiration apparently means ‘breathe again’. This would only serve to confuse students as we try to make a clear distinction between respiration and breathing.

Instead, I would say that respiration is the process by which humans release energy that is stored in glucose. I would say ‘glucose’ instead of ‘food’ because (a) it is more precise and (b) they already know it is the glucose in food that stores energy so we must not revert to using imprecise terminology.

If, however, Energy was covered a while ago, it may be difficult for students to recall and there may be cognitive overload as they try to hold energy stores as well as all the new information in this lesson in their working memory. This problem could be circumvented by asking a question or two about energy stores a few lessons before this one so it helps with slowing the rate of forgetting.

It is important to note that if students have not come across balancing symbol equations by this point, then I would model it explicitly regardless of how good the class is. They may be experts in one concept but not in something they have never encountered before!

In this example of just an introduction to a concept, we have several opportunities to discuss previously learnt concepts and to provide the chance to transfer prior learning. Transfer is an ongoing process but it is worth thinking about what knowledge we need to or can activate in a lesson to help our students learn well.
